stimulus: For decades, biologists assumed that migratory songbirds navigated chiefly by the positions of the stars, since caged birds oriented themselves correctly beneath a planetarium sky. That assumption was complicated when researchers found that the same birds could orient under overcast skies, where no celestial cues were available. Experiments with artificial magnetic fields soon showed that rotating the field around a cage caused the birds to shift their preferred direction by a corresponding angle. Curiously, the birds responded to the inclination of the field lines rather than to their polarity, distinguishing poleward from equatorward rather than north from south. This finding suggested that the avian compass works differently from a human-made one. Later studies located a likely mechanism in light-sensitive proteins of the retina, which may allow birds to perceive the magnetic field as a pattern superimposed on their vision. Most researchers now regard stellar and magnetic cues not as rivals but as complementary systems, with young birds using the stars to calibrate their magnetic sense.

stimulus: When the first planet orbiting a sunlike star was detected in 1995, astronomers were startled by its properties. The planet was roughly half as massive as Jupiter, yet it circled its star in just over four days, far closer than Mercury orbits the Sun. stimulus: Scattered across the plains of northern Europe and North America are boulders whose composition differs sharply from that of the bedrock beneath them. Early naturalists, unable to explain how such massive stones had traveled, often attributed them to a great flood or to icebergs drifting across a submerged continent. In the nineteenth century, geologists familiar with Alpine glaciers proposed a different explanation: that vast ice sheets had once covered these regions and carried the boulders far from their sources. Today the boulders, known as erratics, are routinely used to trace the flow paths of ancient ice sheets.

stimulus: Gresham's law, often summarized as the claim that bad money drives out good, describes what happens when two forms of currency share an official value but differ in intrinsic worth. If a full-weight silver coin and a debased coin containing less silver are both legally worth one unit, people tend to spend the debased coins and to hoard or melt down the full-weight ones. As a result, only the inferior coins remain in everyday circulation. Historians have found many episodes consistent with this pattern, from ancient Rome to early modern England. Yet the law holds only under specific conditions, chiefly that merchants be legally required to accept both coins at the same value. Where traders are free to reject debased coins or to discount them, the reverse can occur, as people come to prefer transacting in the more reliable currency. Some economists therefore argue that the principle is better understood as a consequence of legal price fixing than as a general law of monetary behavior.

stimulus: Among the most robust findings in the psychology of memory is the spacing effect: information studied in several sessions separated by intervals is retained longer than the same information studied in a single concentrated session. The effect was first documented in the late nineteenth century and has since been replicated with materials ranging from vocabulary lists to surgical skills. Despite this record, many students continue to prefer cramming, in part because massed study produces a strong feeling of fluency during the session itself. That feeling is misleading, since performance immediately after study is a poor predictor of performance weeks later. One explanation for the effect holds that spaced repetitions force learners to retrieve partially forgotten material, and that the effort of retrieval strengthens memory traces. Another proposes that spaced sessions encode the material in more varied contexts, providing additional cues for later recall. These accounts are not mutually exclusive, and both may contribute to the advantage.

stimulus: When speakers of mutually unintelligible languages are brought into sustained contact, they often develop a pidgin, a simplified contact language with a limited vocabulary and few grammatical markers. A pidgin has no native speakers; it serves as a practical tool for trade or labor. If children grow up acquiring a pidgin as their first language, however, it may develop into a creole, a full language with a stable grammar. Some linguists have observed that creoles arising in widely separated parts of the world share striking structural features, such as marking tense and aspect with separate particles placed before the verb. They have taken these similarities as evidence of an innate linguistic blueprint that children impose on impoverished input. Critics counter that many shared features can be traced to the languages spoken by the original adult populations, which were often typologically similar. On this view, creole grammar reflects inheritance and contact rather than a universal default.

stimulus: In an influential essay of the 1960s, one anthropologist described hunter-gatherers as the original affluent society, arguing that foragers met their material needs with only a few hours of work each day. The argument drew on time-allocation studies of groups in southern Africa and northern Australia, which seemed to show that subsistence tasks occupied far less time than industrial labor. This portrait overturned an older image of foragers as perpetually on the brink of starvation. stimulus: Whether the language one speaks shapes how one perceives the world has long divided scholars, and color has served as the principal testing ground. A landmark cross-linguistic survey in the late 1960s argued that, although languages differ in how many basic color terms they possess, those terms emerge in a largely fixed order and cluster around the same focal hues, a pattern that seemed to vindicate universalism. Later work complicated this picture without simply reversing it. Speakers of languages that lexically distinguish light from dark blue discriminate between such shades slightly faster than speakers of languages that do not, but the advantage vanishes when participants must simultaneously rehearse a string of digits, a task that occupies verbal working memory. Such a finding is awkward for strong relativists and universalists alike: the former expected deeper effects, the latter none at all.

stimulus: Why do males of many species bear ornaments, such as the peacock's train, that appear to impair survival? One influential answer, the handicap principle, holds that such traits are attractive precisely because they are costly: only a male in excellent condition can afford an extravagant ornament, so the ornament is an honest signal of quality that weaker rivals cannot fake. Later models rescued the idea by making the cost condition-dependent, so that the burden of the ornament falls more heavily on individuals in poor condition. stimulus: The observation that countries rich in natural resources have, on average, grown more slowly than resource-poor countries has come to be known as the resource curse. stimulus: Models of stellar evolution indicate that the young Sun, some four billion years ago, shone about 25 to 30 percent less brightly than it does today. stimulus: In the classic free-choice paradigm, participants rate a set of items, choose between two they rated similarly, and then rate the items again. Typically the chosen item rises in their estimation and the rejected one falls, a pattern long interpreted as evidence that people ease the discomfort of a difficult decision by revaluing the alternatives. Decades after the paradigm was introduced, a methodological critique showed that this spreading of alternatives could arise even if choosing had no effect on preferences at all. Because initial ratings are noisy estimates of underlying preference, a participant's choice reveals information about which item was truly preferred, and later ratings will tend to drift toward those true values. Studies with corrected designs, in which some participants rate both items twice before choosing, have nonetheless continued to find a spreading effect, though usually a smaller one. The original conclusion has thus survived, but its evidential basis has changed: what was once regarded as a decisive demonstration is now recognized as partly artifact.

stimulus: In the earliest years of cinema, most films consisted of a single shot recorded by a stationary camera, and audiences were content simply to watch movement reproduced on a screen. Within little more than a decade, however, filmmakers had developed a set of editing conventions that allowed stories to unfold across many shots without confusing viewers. Chief among these was the principle of continuity, according to which each cut should preserve the spatial and temporal logic of the action. A character who exits the frame on the right, for instance, should enter the next shot from the left, so that the viewer perceives a single uninterrupted movement. Such conventions were not inevitable discoveries but choices, and some later directors deliberately violated them to unsettle audiences. Nevertheless, continuity editing proved so effective that it remains the default grammar of narrative film. Its very success, ironically, has made it nearly invisible: most viewers notice editing only when a filmmaker breaks the rules.

stimulus: The harpsichord, which dominated keyboard music for much of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, produces sound by plucking its strings with small quills. Because the force of the plucking is the same no matter how hard the player strikes the key, a harpsichordist cannot make individual notes louder or softer. This seemingly simple mechanical difference allowed performers to shape a melody through gradual swells and fades. Over the following decades, composers increasingly wrote music that assumed such control, marking their scores with instructions for crescendos and sudden accents. stimulus: The historically informed performance movement began with a seemingly modest aim: to play early music on the instruments, and in the styles, that its composers would have expected. Its practitioners recovered gut strings, valveless horns, and treatises on ornamentation, and in doing so they made familiar works sound strikingly unfamiliar. Critics soon objected, however, that the movement's characteristic appeal to authenticity was conceptually confused. Even if one could reconstruct an eighteenth-century orchestra in every particular, one could not reconstruct an eighteenth-century audience, whose ears had been shaped by music the modern listener has never heard and whose sense of what counted as novel or dissonant has been irretrievably overlaid by later styles. On this view, the sounds of a period performance may be historical, but their effect cannot be. Some performers accepted the criticism and recast their project, describing it not as a restoration of the past but as a contemporary style that happens to draw on historical evidence. stimulus: Collingwood maintained that the historian's proper object is not the outward event but the thought that animated it, and that this thought can be known only by being re-enacted in the historian's own mind. stimulus: Nineteenth-century debates over the restoration of medieval buildings turned on incompatible conceptions of what a monument is. Viollet-le-Duc, who directed the restoration of many French churches, defined restoration as reestablishing a building in a finished state that may never have existed at any given time. His interventions, guided by a rationalist reconstruction of how Gothic builders ought to have solved a given structural problem, frequently replaced authentic but irregular fabric with idealized forms. Ruskin regarded such work as the most total destruction a building could suffer, since the value of an old building lay precisely in the marks left on it by successive generations. For Ruskin, a monument was a document of its own history; for Viollet-le-Duc, it was the imperfect realization of a design. Modern conservation practice is usually said to descend from Ruskin, and its preference for minimal, reversible, and legible intervention bears this out. Yet the very need to decide which historical layers merit preservation reintroduces a judgment about what the building essentially is, the question Viollet-le-Duc answered too confidently but did not invent.
